front: What is a physical unit?
back: A unit is an arbitrarily chosen, internationally accepted reference standard against which a physical quantity is compared. Measurement = numerical measure × unit.

front: Base units vs derived units
back: Base quantities have fundamental units (m, kg, s, A, K, mol, cd). Derived units are combinations of base units (e.g. newton = kg m s^-2).

front: The seven SI base units
back: metre (length), kilogram (mass), second (time), ampere (current), kelvin (temperature), mole (amount of substance), candela (luminous intensity).

front: Units of plane angle and solid angle (and are they dimensionless?)
back: Plane angle: radian (rad). Solid angle: steradian (sr). Both are ratios (arc/radius, area/radius^2) so both are dimensionless.

front: How are the metre and second defined in the 2018 SI?
back: Second ↔ caesium-133 hyperfine frequency 9,192,631,770 Hz. Metre ↔ speed of light c = 299,792,458 m/s (and kg ↔ Planck constant h).

front: Definition of significant figures
back: Significant digits = reliable digits plus the first uncertain digit of the report, e.g. 1.62 s has 3 sig. figs (1, 6 reliable; 2 uncertain).

front: Do leading zeros count as significant?
back: No — leading zeros after the decimal point (0.007) are not significant. Zeros between non-zero digits always count.

front: Do trailing zeros count?
back: Only with a decimal point: 3.500 has 4 sig. figs; 4700 mm has 2 sig. figs (unless written in scientific notation). Change of units never changes the count.

front: Sig-fig rule for multiplication and division
back: Keep as many significant figures as the input with the LEAST significant figures (division by the volume 2.51 cm^3 limited the density to 3 sig. figs).

front: Sig-fig rule for addition and subtraction
back: Keep as many DECIMAL PLACES as the input with the least decimal places. E.g. 436.32 + 227.2 + 0.301 = 663.8 g (one decimal place).

front: Rounding off the uncertain digit
back: Dropped digit > 5 → raise the preceding digit; < 5 → leave it. Exactly 5 → drop if preceding digit is even, raise by 1 if it is odd (2.745 → 2.74, 2.735 → 2.74).

front: How to handle intermediate values in multi-step calculations
back: Retain one digit more than the significant digits in intermediate steps and round off only at the end, to avoid accumulation of rounding errors.

front: Product rule for relative errors
back: In multiplication/division the relative errors ADD. (16.2 ± 0.1)cm × (10.1 ± 0.1)cm → area = 163.62 ± 1.6% = 164 ± 3 cm^2.

front: Define the dimensions of a physical quantity
back: The powers to which the base quantities are raised to represent the quantity, e.g. force [M L T^-2]. Dimensions carry no magnitudes.

front: Dimensions of velocity, acceleration, force, density, energy
back: v: [L T^-1]; a: [L T^-2]; F = ma: [M L T^-2]; ρ = m/V: [M L^-3]; Energy/work: [M L^2 T^-2].

front: Dimensional formula vs dimensional equation
back: Dimensional formula = how base quantities represent the dimensions. Dimensional equation = the physical quantity equated to its dimensional formula, e.g. [V] = [M^0 L^3 T^0].

front: Principle of homogeneity of dimensions
back: An equation is correct only if every term on both sides has the same dimensions. Dimensionless arguments are required for trig, log and exponential functions.

front: If an equation passes the dimensional test, is it certainly right?
back: No. Failing the test proves it WRONG; passing only shows dimensional consistency — dimensionless factors (like 2π) may hide, so it is not proved right.

front: Method of dimensions: what relation does it give for the pendulum period T?
back: Assuming T = k·l^x·g^y·m^z gives T = k·sqrt(l/g). The constant k (actually 2π) cannot be found by dimensions; the period is independent of the bob mass.

front: Limitations of dimensional analysis (3)
back: (1) Cannot find dimensionless constants like 2π. (2) Cannot decide between formulas with identical dimensions. (3) Cannot distinguish same-dimensional quantities (work vs torque).

front: Order of magnitude of the Earth vs a hydrogen atom
back: Earth ~ 1.28 x 10^7 m (order 10^7), H atom ~ 1.06 x 10^-10 m (order 10^-10). The Earth is 17 orders of magnitude larger.

front: Useful conversions: 1 ly, 1 Å, 1 cal x J
back: 1 light year = 9.46 x 10^15 m; 1 Ångström = 10^-10 m; 1 calorie ~ 4.2 J (1 J = 1 kg m^2 s^-2).

front: How to estimate the diameter of a thread with a thread and metre scale
back: Wind the thread tightly around a pencil or cylinder; measure the length covered by many turns and divide by the number of turns.

front: Which length-measuring device is most precise and why?
back: An optical device measuring to within a wavelength of light — its least count (resolution) is the finest, far better than vernier callipers (0.01 cm) or a micrometer screw gauge.

front: Sun's average density estimate
back: M = 2 x 10^30 kg, R = 7 x 10^8 m → ρ = M/(4/3)πR^3 ~ 1.4 x 10^3 kg m^-3, close to liquid density because the core is intensely compressed.
